abstract: Abstract The Mondo family transcription factor MondoA plays a pivotal role in sensing metabolites, such as glucose, glutamine, and lactic acid, to regulate glucose metabolism and cell proliferation. Ketone bodies are important signals for reducing glucose uptake. However, it is unclear whether MondoA functions in ketone body‐regulated glucose transport. Here we reported that ketone bodies promoted MondoA nuclear translocation and binding to the promoter of its target gene TXNIP. Ketone bodies reduced glucose uptake, increased apoptosis and decreased proliferation of colorectal cancer cells, which was impeded by MondoA knockdown. Moreover, we identified MEK1 as a novel component of the MondoA protein complex using a proteomic approach. Mechanistically, MEK1 interacted with MondoA and enhanced tyrosine 222, but not serine or threonine, phosphorylation of MondoA, inhibiting MondoA nuclear translocation and transcriptional activity. Ketone bodies decreased MEK1‐dependent MondoA phosphorylation by blocking MondoA and MEK1 interaction, leading to MondoA nuclear translocation, TXNIP transcription, and inhibition of glucose uptake. Therefore, our study not only demonstrated that ketone bodies reduce glucose uptake, promote apoptosis, and inhibit cell proliferation in colorectal cancer cells by regulating MondoA phosphorylation but also identified MEK1‐dependent phosphorylation as a new mechanism to manipulate MondoA activity.

MATERIALS AND METHODS
2.1
Plasmids
Human MondoA cDNA was kindly provided by Dr Donald Ayer (University of Utah) and cloned into the pcDNA3 vector (Clontech) and doxycycline‐inducible lentiviral vector pLUT. Human MEK1 or MEK2 cDNA was obtained from Dharmacon and cloned into the pIRESpuro vector (LifeTechnologies). Point mutations were generated using the KOD‐Plus‐Mutagenesis Kit (Toyobo).
2.2
Cell culture and treatment
RKO, SW480 human colorectal cancer cells, 293T human embryonic kidney cells, HeLa human cervical cancer cells, and C2C12 mouse skeletal myoblast cells were obtained from the Cell Bank of Chinese Academy of Sciences and maintained at 37°C in DMEM (Hyclone). For β‐hydroxybutyrate treatment, cells were cultured in DMEM containing 5.6 mM glucose and then treated with 5 mM β‐hydroxybutyrate (Sigma‐Aldrich) for 4 h.
2.3
ShRNA
transfection
The shRNAs (Sangon) were subcloned into the lentiviral vector PLKO and transfected into 293T cells with PMD2G and psPAX2. Supernatants containing viruses were collected and infected with RKO and SW480 cell lines. ShRNA sequences are listed in Table
S1
.
2.4
Quantitative
PCR
(
QPCR
)
Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol (LifeTechnologies). CDNA was synthesized using a GoScript reverse transcription kit (Takara). Quantitative PCR was performed using SYBR Premix Ex Taq (Takara). Primer sequences are listed in Table
S2
.
2.5
Chromatin immunoprecipitation
Cells were fixed in 1% paraformaldehyde. Chromatin was sheared using sonication to create 150–300 bp fragments and immunoprecipitated with anti‐IgG (MBL), anti‐MondoA (Bethyl Laboratories), or anti‐Flag (MBL) antibodies. Quantitative PCR was performed using the SYBR Premix Ex Taq (Takara). Primer sequences are listed in Table
S3
.
For more materials and methods used in this study, please refer to the Supplementary Materials and Methods
S1
.

1
INTRODUCTION
MondoA and its paralog carbohydrate response element binding protein (ChREBP, also named MondoB) belong to the basic helix–loop–helix leucine zipper (bHLH/LZ) transcription factor family.
1
,
2
MondoA promotes transcription of thioredoxin interacting protein (TXNIP) which encodes the protein to restrict glucose uptake by increasing internalization of the glucose transporter 1 (Glut1) and decreasing the transcription of Glut1.
3
,
4
MondoA functions as a sensor of intracellular metabolites. Glucose increases MondoA expression, promoting its nuclear translocation and binding to the carbohydrate response element (ChoRE) of target genes.
5
Glutamine inhibits MondoA transcriptional activity and increases glucose uptake and aerobic glycolysis.
6
Lactic acidosis activates the MondoA‐TXNIP pathway, leading to reduced glucose uptake.
7
Although MondoA serves as the metabolite sensor, it remains largely unclear how transcriptional activity of MondoA is regulated.
Ketone bodies, including β‐hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate and acetone, are metabolites serving as an alternative energy source to glucose. Ketone bodies play an important role in regulating the nucleo‐cytosolic trafficking and transcriptional activity of ChREBP, a paralog of MondoA.
8
It is unclear whether ketone bodies influence MondoA activity. Notably, ketone bodies have been reported to oppose initiation and growth of some cancers, including breast cancer, glioma, and gastric cancer.
9
,
10
In addition, acetoacetate reduces cell growth in human colorectal cancer cell lines.
11
Growth of colon cancer cells is delayed by ketogenic diet.
12
,
13
However, the mechanism by which ketone bodies inhibit proliferation of colorectal cancer cells is not fully understood.
The Ras–Raf–MEK–ERK pathway modulates several aspects of tumor development, including proliferation, invasion, and metastasis. The Ras–Raf–MEK–ERK pathway is hyperactive in many types of human cancer, such as colorectal cancer, melanoma, and pancreatic cancer.
14
,
15
,
16
,
17
MEK plays a critical role in proliferation and metabolism of colorectal cancer cells.
18
,
19
MEK inhibitor PD325901 significantly decreases glucose consumption and lactate production.
20
MEK increases the expression of lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA), leading to colorectal cancer cell growth.
21
In addition, Ras‐MAPK signaling actively inhibits TXNIP expression while MEK inhibitor U0126 restores TXNIP protein levels.
22
However, the molecular mechanism underlying MEK‐mediated TXNIP regulation remains to be determined.
In our study, we found that ketone bodies promoted MondoA nuclear translocation and TXNIP transcription, reduced glucose uptake, increased apoptosis, and decreased the proliferation of colorectal cancer cells. Moreover, MEK1 interacted with MondoA, leading to its tyrosine phosphorylation at tyrosine 222 and inactivation. Therefore, we identified the novel role of MEK1‐dependent phosphorylation in regulating MondoA activity and demonstrated that MondoA‐TXNIP played an important role in ketone body‐induced proliferation inhibition in colorectal cancer cells. Our research will provide a new therapeutic option against colorectal cancers.

3
RESULTS
3.1
Ketone bodies stimulate
TXNIP
expression, reduce glucose uptake, promote apoptosis, and inhibit cell proliferation in colorectal cancer cells
To investigate whether ketone bodies influence MondoA activity, we treated SW480 human colorectal cancer cells with control (PBS) or β‐hydroxybutyrate of different concentrations (1, 2.5, 5 and 10 mM) for 4 h. We chose β‐hydroxybutyrate as the representative ketone body because it accounts for approximately 78% of the ketone bodies in serum.
23
We found that compared with the control, 5 and 10 mM β‐hydroxybutyrate did not change MondoA mRNA abundance but increased its target gene TXNIP transcription (Figure
S1A
). In humans, the level of ketone bodies in serum is around 0.05–0.1 mM, reaching 6–8 mM after prolonged starvation
24
and 20–25 mM during diabetic ketoacidosis.
25
Therefore, we chose 5 mM as the treatment concentration in the rest of our experiments. We found TXNIP mRNA and protein levels were induced by β‐hydroxybutyrate compared with PBS in RKO human colorectal cancer cells (Figure
1A–C
). Furthermore, since MondoA was highly expressed in skeletal muscle,
26
we treated C2C12 mouse skeletal myoblast cells with β‐hydroxybutyrate and found that β‐hydroxybutyrate increased TXNIP mRNA and protein levels in differentiated and undifferentiated C2C12 cells (Figure
1D–F
). In addition, we found that ketone bodies induced TXNIP expression in a time‐dependent manner (Figure
S1C,D
). These finding suggested that ketone bodies induced expression of TXNIP in different cell types.
FIGURE 1
Ketone bodies promote TXNIP expression and reduce glucose uptake. (A) QPCR analysis of MondoA and TXNIP mRNA levels in RKO human colorectal cancer cells treated with PBS or 5 mM β‐hydroxybutyrate (β‐HB) for 4 h. (B) Immunoblot analysis of endogenous MondoA and TXNIP protein levels in RKO cells treated with PBS or 5 mM β‐HB for 4 h. (C) Quantitative analysis of protein levels in Figure
1B
. (D) QPCR analysis of MondoA and TXNIP mRNA levels in undifferentiated and differentiated C2C12 murine skeletal muscle cells treated with PBS or 5 mM β‐HB for 4 h. (E) Immunoblot analysis of endogenous TXNIP levels in undifferentiated and differentiated C2C12 cells treated with PBS or 5 mM β‐HB for 4 h. (F) Quantitative analysis of protein levels in (E). (G) Glucose consumption of RKO human colorectal cancer cells treated with PBS or 5 mM β‐HB for 24 h.
Given that TXNIP acted as a potent negative regulator of glucose uptake,
3
,
4
we analyzed glucose consumption by calculating the reduction in glucose concentration of the medium and by directly measuring glucose incorporation using a fluorescent glucose analog, 2‐(N‐[7‐nitrobenz‐2‐oxa‐1,3‐diazol‐4‐yl] amino)‐2‐deoxyglucose (2‐NBDG). As expected, TXNIP induction by β‐hydroxybutyrate was accompanied by a decrease in glucose uptake (Figure
S1B
and Figure
1G
). We further separated the membrane and cytoplasmic protein fractions and observed that ketone bodies decreased Glut1 and Glut4 expression in the cell membrane fraction compared with controls in RKO human colorectal cancer cells (Figure
S1E,F
).
We next investigated whether ketone bodies affected colorectal cancer cell proliferation. We compared cell numbers at days 2, 4, and 6 after treating SW480 cells with PBS or β‐hydroxybutyrate and observed that ketone bodies resulted in reduction in cell growth (Figure
S1G
). To further test whether β‐hydroxybutyrate‐induced TXNIP expression led to the induction of apoptosis, we treated SW480 human colorectal cancer cells with either PBS or β‐hydroxybutyrate. Annexin‐V/propidium iodide (PI) staining showed that β‐hydroxybutyrate resulted in a significant increase in the percentage of early apoptotic (Annexin
+
/PI
−
) and late apoptotic/necrotic (Annexin
+
/PI
+
) cells (Figure
S1H
). Therefore, our research demonstrated that ketone bodies stimulated TXNIP expression, reduced glucose uptake, promoted apoptosis and retarded proliferation in colorectal cancer cells.
3.2
MondoA
plays an important role in
TXNIP
activation, glucose uptake reduction, apoptosis, and growth inhibition of colorectal cancer cells in response to ketone bodies
TXNIP expression is highly dependent on MondoA.
27
To evaluate the involvement of MondoA in TXNIP transcriptional activation in response to ketone bodies, we generated RKO and SW480 cells stably transfected with short hairpin RNA (shRNA) for MondoA. We treated these cells with either PBS or β‐hydroxybutyrate for 4 h and analyzed MondoA and its target genes mRNA and protein levels. Quantitative RT‐PCR and western blot showed that knockdown of MondoA blocked ketone body‐dependent TXNIP induction (Figure
2A–F
), suggesting MondoA played an important role in ketone body‐induced TXNIP transcriptional activation.
FIGURE 2
MondoA plays an important role in ketone body‐induced TXNIP activation and glucose uptake reduction. (A) QPCR analysis of MondoA and TXNIP mRNA levels in RKO human colorectal cancer cells stably expressing either control (shNC) or MondoA shRNAs, followed by treatment with PBS or 5 mM β‐hydroxybutyrate (β‐HB) for 4 h. (B) QPCR analysis of MondoA and TXNIP mRNA levels in SW480 human colorectal cancer cells stably expressing either control (shNC) or MondoA shRNAs, followed by treatment with PBS or 5 mM β‐HB for 4 h. (C) Immunoblot analysis of endogenous MondoA and TXNIP protein levels in RKO cells stably expressing either control (shNC) or MondoA shRNAs, followed by treatment with PBS or 5 mM β‐HB for 4 h. (D) Immunoblot analysis of endogenous MondoA and TXNIP protein levels in SW480 cells stably expressing either control (shNC) or MondoA shRNAs, followed by treatment with PBS or 5 mM β‐HB for 4 h. (E) Quantitative analysis of protein levels in (C). (F) Quantitative analysis of protein levels in (D). (G) Glucose uptake analysis of SW480 cells stably expressing either control (shNC) or MondoA shRNAs, followed by treatment with PBS or 5 mM β‐HB for 4 h.
Since the MondoA‐TXNIP axis functioned to limit glucose uptake,
3
,
4
we performed 2‐NBDG assay to compare the glucose uptake of control and MondoA knockdown cells after PBS or β‐hydroxybutyrate treatment. We observed that knockdown of MondoA blocked ketone body‐induced inhibition of glucose uptake, which suggested that MondoA sensed ketone bodies to trigger a TXNIP‐dependent inhibition of glucose uptake (Figure
2G
). We next determined whether MondoA mediated the antiproliferative effects of ketone bodies. We compared growth kinetics by counting cell numbers at days 2, 4, and 6 after PBS or β‐hydroxybutyrate treatment. We found that MondoA knockdown abolished the reduction in colorectal cancer cell growth by ketone bodies (Figure
S2A
). Moreover, quantitative PCR and western blot showed that MondoA knockdown attenuated the upregulation of Bax and caspase‐3 cleavage by ketone bodies (Figure
S2B–E
).These results revealed that MondoA played an important role in ketone body‐induced TXNIP upregulation, glucose uptake restriction, cell apoptosis, and growth inhibition in colorectal cancer cells.
3.3
Ketone bodies increase the nuclear abundance and
DNA
binding activity of
MondoA
Mondo family transcription factors can alter their transcriptional activity by changing the subcellular localization and DNA‐binding activity.
28
,
29
,
30
To delineate the mechanism by which ketone bodies increased MondoA transcriptional activity, we separated the nuclear and cytoplasmic protein fractions from PBS or β‐hydroxybutyrate‐treated SW480 cells, and found that ketone bodies promoted MondoA nuclear translocation (Figure
3A,B
). To illustrate whether ketone bodies altered MondoA binding to the TXNIP promoter, we treated SW480 cells with PBS or β‐hydroxybutyrate for 4 h and performed chromatin immunoprecipitation analysis. Quantitative PCR analysis showed that β‐hydroxybutyrate promoted endogenous MondoA binding to TXNIP promoter (Figure
3C
). β‐hydroxybutyrate can regulate epigenetic modifications, including histone acetylation and β‐hydroxybutyrylation.
31
,
32
We performed a chromatin‐immunoprecipitation assay using the anti‐acetylated histone H3 lysine 9 (H3K9ac), anti‐acetylated histone H3 lysine 27 (H3K27ac), anti‐β‐hydroxybutyrylated H3 lysine 9 (H3K9bhb), or isotype control antibodies. We did not observe obvious differences in acetylation or β‐hydroxybutyrylation of histones for the TXNIP promoter between control (PBS) and β‐hydroxybutyrate‐treated SW480 human colorectal cancer cells, suggesting that epigenetic modifications might not be the primary cause for TXNIP induction by β‐hydroxybutyrate (Figure
3D,E
). To sum up, we revealed that ketone bodies increased the nuclear localization and binding activity of MondoA to stimulate TXNIP expression.
FIGURE 3
Ketone bodies increase nuclear abundance and DNA binding activity of MondoA. (A) Nuclear and cytosolic fractionation analysis showed that β‐hydroxybutyrate (β‐HB) promoted MondoA nuclear translocation. (B) Quantitative analysis of protein levels in Figure
3A
. (C) Chromatin immunoprecipitation analysis showed that β‐HB promoted MondoA binding to the TXNIP promoter. (D) Chromatin immunoprecipitation analysis showed that β‐HB did not change the acetylation of histones for the TXNIP promoter. (E) Chromatin immunoprecipitation analysis showed that β‐HB did not change the β‐hydroxybutyrylation of histones for the TXNIP promoter.
3.4
MondoA
interacts with
MEK1
and
MEK2
Phosphorylation retains ChREBP, the other member of the Mondo family, in the cytoplasm and renders it inactive,
33
,
34
,
35
,
36
,
37
but phosphorylation of MondoA has not been reported so far. To examine the molecular mechanisms by which ketone bodies increased the activity of MondoA, we used a proteomic approach to identify proteins interacting with MondoA. 293T cells stably transfected with a doxycycline‐inducible plasmid containing Flag‐tagged MondoA were treated with doxycycline to induce MondoA protein expression. Silver staining showed enrichment of MondoA and its interacting proteins in the Flag‐MondoA eluates compared to untreated or parental controls (Figure
4A
). Eluates were then subjected to multidimensional protein identification technology (MudPIT) analysis. Mlx and 14‐3‐3, already known MondoA interacting proteins, were identified, which demonstrated the efficacy of our approach in identifying interaction partners of MondoA. Interestingly, we identified a number of peptides from MEK1 and MEK2, two kinases that can phosphorylate serine, threonine, and tyrosine residues of proteins (Figure
4B
).
FIGURE 4
MondoA interacts with MEK1 and MEK2. (A) Silver‐staining analysis for 293T cell lysates immunoprecipitated with the anti‐Flag antibody. The arrow points to the protein band of Flag‐MondoA. Parental 293T and 293T cells stably transfected with the doxycycline‐inducible plasmid containing Flag‐MondoA and treated with (+Dox) or without doxycycline (−Dox) were analyzed. (B) MudPIT analyses of the relative abundance of MondoA and highly enriched proteins by mass spectrometry. (C) Immunofluorescent staining of endogenous MondoA and MEK1/2 in HeLa human cervical cancer cells. The scale bar was 20 μm. (D) Co‐immunoprecipitation analysis of ectopically expressed Myc‐tagged GFP, MEK1, MEK2, and endogenous MondoA in 293T cells. (E) Co‐immunoprecipitation analysis of ectopically expressed Flag‐tagged MondoA and endogenous MEK1/2 in 293T cells. The arrow points to MEK1/2 protein bands. (F) Co‐immunoprecipitation analysis of endogenous MondoA and MEK1/2 in human colorectal cancer SW480 cells. The arrow points to MEK1/2 protein bands.
To determine whether MondoA co‐localized with MEK1/2, we performed immunofluorescent staining and found that exogenous MEK1 and MEK2 co‐localized with MondoA (Figure
S3C,D
). Furthermore, endogenous MondoA also co‐localized with MEK1/2 (Figure
4C
). We next tried to validate the interaction between MondoA and MEK1/2 using co‐immunoprecipitation. We found that exogenous MEK1 and MEK2 co‐immunoprecipitated with endogenous MondoA (Figure
4D
) and exogenous MondoA co‐immunoprecipitated with endogenous MEK1/2 (Figure
4E
). In addition, endogenous MondoA and MEK1/2 proteins co‐immunoprecipitated in SW480 cells (Figure
4F
). We further analyzed MondoA and MEK1 subcellular localization in the presence and absence of ketone bodies in RKO cells. We found that compared with PBS, β‐hydroxybutyrate promoted the nuclear localization of MondoA and had no obvious effect on that of MEK1 in RKO cells (Figure
S3E
). Together, we concluded that MondoA interacted with MEK1 and MEK2.
3.5
MEK1
enhances tyrosine phosphorylation of
MondoA
and tyrosine 222 is the main phosphorylation site of
MondoA
MEK1/2 are dual specific protein kinases that can phosphorylate serine, threonine, and tyrosine residues of proteins. MEK1/2 phosphorylate extracellular signal‐regulated kinases (ERK) at threonine and tyrosine residues.
38
To explore whether MEK1 or MEK2 functions as a kinase to regulate MondoA phosphorylation, we overexpressed Myc‐MEK1 or Myc‐MEK2 in 293T cells, immunoprecipitated endogenous MondoA proteins and immunoblotted with the anti‐pan‐phospho‐serine/threonine or tyrosine antibody to detect phosphorylated MondoA. We found that MEK1, but not MEK2, increased MondoA tyrosine phosphorylation, whereas no serine/threonine phosphorylation was observed (Figure
5A,B
). Interestingly, when Flag‐tagged truncated MondoA (N‐terminal 1–325 amino acids, named as N‐Flag‐MondoA), Myc‐MEK1, and Myc‐MEK2 were transiently expressed in 293T cells, double bands of MondoA were observed. The upper band nearly disappeared after λ‐protein phosphatase treatment (Figure
5C
), indicating it was the phosphorylated N‐Flag‐MondoA. We further found that MEK1, but not MEK2, enhanced phosphorylation of N‐terminal MondoA (Figure
5D
). In addition, we performed in vitro kinase assays using the recombinant His‐MEK1 and Flag‐MondoA purified from 293T cells, immunoblotted with the anti‐pan‐phospho‐tyrosine antibody and observed that MondoA was directly phosphorylated by recombinant MEK1 (Figure
S4A
).
FIGURE 5
MEK1 phosphorylates MondoA at tyrosine 222. (A) MEK1 phosphorylated MondoA at tyrosine but not serine/threonine sites. 293T human embryonic kidney cells were transfected with plasmids containing control, Myc‐MEK1 or Myc‐MEK2, followed by immunoprecipitation for MondoA and immunoblot with the anti‐pan‐phospho‐serine/threonine (p‐Ser/Thr) or anti‐phospho‐tyrosine (p‐Tyr) antibody. (B) Quantitative analysis of protein levels in (A). (C) Immunoblot analysis showed that MondoA displayed double bands when MEK1, MEK2, and N‐terminal MondoA were co‐expressed in 293T cells and the upper band was abolished by λ phosphatase treatment. (D) Immunoblot analysis showed that it was MEK1, not MEK2, that enhanced the abundance of the upper band of N‐terminal MondoA. (E) Immunoblot analysis showed that the upper band of N‐terminal MondoA was abolished by Y222F mutation. (F) Y222F mutation abolished MondoA phosphorylation at tyrosine sites. 293T cells were transfected with plasmids containing Flag‐MondoA or Flag‐MondoA‐Y222F, followed by immunoprecipitation for MondoA and immunoblot with the anti‐pan‐phospho‐tyrosine antibody. (G) Quantitative analysis of protein levels in (F). (H) Co‐immunoprecipitation analysis showed that Y222F mutation decreased MondoA and MEK1 interaction.
We next performed site‐directed mutations of putative phosphorylation sites of N‐terminal of MondoA, which were predicted according to the PhosphoSitePlus website (
https://www.phosphosite.org/homeAction.action
) and found that the upper band of MondoA was almost abolished by Y222F mutation (Figure
5E
). According to the domain structure of MondoA,
39
tyrosine 222 was located near the nuclear localization signal of MondoA. Multiple sequence alignment of MondoA from different species indicated the sequence surrounding tyrosine 222 was conserved from
Danio rerio
to
Homo sapiens
(Figure
S4B
). Moreover, we overexpressed Flag‐tagged MondoA and dephosphomimic mutant MondoA‐Y222F in 293T cells, immunoprecipitated with anti‐Flag antibody followed by western blot analysis and found that MondoA‐Y222F proteins displayed reduced basal tyrosine phosphorylation compared with WT (Figure
5F,G
). In addition, we overexpressed Myc‐MEK1, Flag‐MondoA and Flag‐MondoA‐Y222F in 293T cells, performed co‐immunoprecipitation experiment and observed that Y222F mutation substantially decreased MondoA and MEK1 interaction (Figure
5H
). These results indicated that MEK1 phosphorylated MondoA and tyrosine 222 of MondoA was its main phosphorylation site.
3.6
Dephosphorylation stimulates
MondoA
transcriptional activity
Subcellular localization and transcriptional activity of ChREBP, the MondoA paralog, are regulated by its phosphorylation status.
33
,
34
,
35
,
36
,
37
To investigate whether phosphorylation modulates MondoA subcellular localization, we transfected 293T cells with WT and MondoA‐Y222F, and cell fractionation analysis showed that dephosphomimic mutation Y222F increased MondoA nuclear translocation (Figure
6A,B
). To examine the effect of the Y222F mutation on MondoA binding activity, we ectopically expressed WT and MondoA‐Y222F in 293T cells and performed chromatin immunoprecipitation analysis. We found that the Y222F mutation increased MondoA DNA binding activity (Figure
6C
). Moreover, quantitative PCR and western blot analysis confirmed that MondoA‐Y222F overexpression resulted in increased mRNA transcription and protein expression of TXNIP (Figure
6D–F
). Taken together, these data suggested that dephosphorylation of MondoA at tyrosine 222 increased its transcriptional activity.
FIGURE 6
Dephosphorylation promotes MondoA transcriptional activity. (A) Nuclear and cytosolic fractionation analysis showed that Y222F mutation stimulated MondoA nuclear translocation. (B) Quantitative analysis of protein levels in (A). (C) Chromatin immunoprecipitation analysis showed that Y222F mutation promoted DNA‐binding activity of MondoA. (D) QPCR analysis of MondoA and TXNIP mRNA levels at 48 h after transfecting 293T cells with plasmids containing control, Flag‐MondoA or Flag‐MondoA‐Y222F. (E) Immunoblot analysis of MondoA and TXNIP protein levels at 48 h after transfecting 293T cells with plasmids containing control, Flag‐MondoA, or Flag‐MondoA‐Y222F. (F) Quantitative analysis of protein levels in (E).
3.7
Ketone bodies decrease
MondoA
,
MEK1,
and 14‐3‐3 interaction
To investigate the role of MondoA phosphorylation in response to ketone bodies, we overexpressed Flag‐MondoA in 293T cells, followed by PBS or β‐hydroxybutyrate treatment. We found that β‐hydroxybutyrate decreased MondoA tyrosine phosphorylation (Figure
7A
). To study whether ketone bodies altered MEK/ERK signaling, we treated RKO cells with PBS or β‐hydroxybutyrate and compared the level of phosphorylated ERK1/2. Compared with the control, β‐hydroxybutyrate did not change phosphorylation of ERK (Figure
S4C,D
). We next investigate whether ketone bodies affected the interaction between MEK1 and MondoA. We transfected 293T cells with Myc‐MEK1 and treated cells with PBS or β‐hydroxybutyrate. Co‐immunoprecipitation studies revealed that ketone bodies reduced MondoA and MEK1 interaction (Figure
7B
). Moreover, we treated RKO cells with PBS or β‐hydroxybutyrate in the presence or absence of MEK inhibitor U0126. We found that U0126 reduced the effect of ketone bodies on TXNIP activation, MondoA nuclear translocation, and growth inhibition in colorectal cancer cells, suggesting that MEK activity played an important role (Figure
S4E–H
). Our results suggested that ketone bodies decreased MEK1‐dependent MondoA phosphorylation by blocking MondoA and MEK1 interaction.
FIGURE 7
Ketone bodies decrease MondoA phosphorylation and reduce MondoA, MEK1, and 14‐3‐3 interaction. (A) β‐hydroxybutyrate (β‐HB) treatment decreased MondoA phosphorylation at tyrosine sites. (B) Co‐immunoprecipitation analysis of the interaction between the interaction between ectopically expressed MEK1 and endogenous MondoA in 293T cells treated with PBS or 5 mM β‐HB for 4 h. (C) Co‐immunoprecipitation analysis of the interaction between ectopically expressed 14‐3‐3β and endogenous MondoA in 293T cells treated with PBS or 5 mM β‐HB for 4 h. (D) Co‐immunoprecipitation analysis of the interaction of endogenous MondoA, MEK1, and 14‐3‐3 in RKO cells treated with PBS or 5 mM β‐HB for 4 h. (E) Schematic diagram showing that ketone bodies decreased MEK1‐dependent MondoA phosphorylation by blocking MondoA and MEK1 interaction, leading to MondoA nuclear translocation, TXNIP transcription, and inhibition of glucose uptake.
14‐3‐3 interacts with MondoA and contributes to the cytoplasmic retention of MondoA.
40
To explore whether ketone bodies changed MondoA and 14‐3‐3 interaction, we transfected Flag‐14‐3‐3 β in 293T cells, and treated cells with PBS or β‐hydroxybutyrate. Co‐immunoprecipitation analysis showed that ketone bodies reduced MondoA and 14‐3‐3 β interaction (Figure
7C
). Furthermore, we observed that ketone bodies reduced endogenous MondoA, 14‐3‐3, and MEK1 interaction in RKO cells (Figure
7D
). To examine the localization of the MEK1, MondoA, and 14‐3‐3 in response to ketone bodies, we separated the nuclear and cytoplasmic protein fractions from PBS or β‐hydroxybutyrate‐treated RKO cells. We observed that MEK1 and 14‐3‐3 were predominantly localized in the cytoplasm and β‐hydroxybutyrate did not affect MEK1 and 14‐3‐3 subcellular localization, whereas MondoA was mainly localized in the cytoplasm and translocated into the nucleus upon β‐hydroxybutyrate treatment (Figure
S3A,B
). These results suggested that ketone bodies decreased MEK1‐mediated MondoA tyrosine phosphorylation, reducing the interaction between MondoA and MEK1 or 14‐3‐3, thus promoting MondoA nuclear translocation and DNA binding. (Figure
7E
).
4
DISCUSSION
Here we revealed the novel role of MondoA in sensing the level of intracellular ketone bodies in colorectal cancer cells. Ketone bodies induced MondoA activation by regulating the interaction between MondoA and MEK1 as well as MEK1‐dependent MondoA phosphorylation. Therefore, our work not only identified the long‐sought mechanism for MondoA phosphorylation but also provided a novel role of MondoA‐TXNIP in sensing ketone bodies to reduce glucose uptake and cell proliferation.
MondoA plays an important role in sensing metabolites, regulating glucose uptake and cell proliferation. TXNIP is a direct target of MondoA that triggers a negative feedback loop by restricting glucose uptake when glucose levels increase, suggesting a critical role of MondoA‐TXNIP in maintaining glucose homeostasis.

However, we did not find obvious differences in acetylation or β‐hydroxybutyrylation of histones for the TXNIP promoter between the control (PBS) and β‐hydroxybutyrate‐treated SW480 human colorectal cancer cells. Whether β‐HB induces epigenetic changes at other cis‐regulatory regions other than the promoter of the TXNIP gene requires further investigation.
Post‐translational modifications, especially phosphorylation, are important for subcellular localization and transcriptional activity of ChREBP, the other Mondo family transcription factor. However, phosphorylation of MondoA has not been reported yet. Using a proteomic analysis, we identified kinase MEK1 as a novel component of the MondoA protein complex. We found that MEK1 interacted with MondoA and enhanced tyrosine phosphorylation of MondoA. We also identified tyrosine 222 of MondoA as its main phosphorylation site. Furthermore, we uncovered that phosphorylation status was responsible for the regulation of MondoA. Dephosphomimic mutation Y222F decreased MondoA phosphorylation and promoted MondoA nuclear translocation and transcriptional activity. Therefore, we have revealed the molecular mechanism by which the upstream signal, ketone bodies, regulate MondoA activity, reduce glucose uptake, promote apoptosis and inhibit cell proliferation in colorectal cancer cells. Moreover, the phosphatase of MondoA and the physiological/pathological significance of MondoA phosphorylation await further study.
Our study has not only demonstrated that ketone bodies reduce glucose uptake, promote apoptosis, and inhibit cell proliferation in colorectal cancer cells by regulating MondoA phosphorylation and activation but also identified MEK1‐dependent phosphorylation as a new mechanism to manipulate MondoA activity. Our research will provide new strategies and targets for colorectal cancer prevention and treatment.
